text: A separate persistence check fingerprints selected product and transaction rows before and after an application restart and finds all thirty-four rows equal. This supports the ordinary persistence of those records, but it is not a test of backup restoration, disk failure or full database recovery. Sessions behave differently: in-process login state may be lost on restart even though stock data persists.
Traceability and validity of the conclusions
display: 5.7 Traceability and validity of the conclusions

text: The evidence is strongest where a requirement maps to a direct assertion: non-negative stock under concurrency is checked through the final balance and the number of successes, exact replay through the identifier and quantity, batch allocation through sellable balances and remainders, purchase approval through recheck, receipt and replay assertions, and acknowledgement and review through reviewer and snapshot checks. Sustained multi-user workload, supplier integration and operational usability, by contrast, have weak or no evidence and are reported as such.

Internal validity is limited by the chosen test scenarios and the execution environment, and external validity by the demonstration data and the single-store boundary. Construct validity depends on measuring what is intended: movement counts are not sales, current-price value is not profit, and the latency of one sequential query is not throughput capacity. The figures and result tables observe these distinctions throughout.

In summary, the evidence supports the specified stock, authorization, warning and recovery behavior in local single-store scenarios. Generalizing beyond them is limited by synthetic data, selected concurrency patterns and a sequential benchmark of a single read operation. Production capacity, reduced stockouts and employee usability would require broader workloads and evaluation in an operating store, and deployment security and recovery would need assessment beyond a cache interruption and a process restart.
Chapter summary

Functional tests support the implemented stock arithmetic, audit path, role boundaries and warning transitions, and browser evidence supports the rendered workflow and selected end-to-end journeys. Under a small sequential workload, the cache-enabled warning query shows a lower pooled median latency, and the failure records support the cache fallback and ordinary persistence. The conclusion relates these findings to the research questions and outlines the work needed for a broader deployment.
Conclusion

Shelfwise implements an inventory and stock-warning workflow for a single supermarket. The application ties each product balance to the stock movements that produced it and ties each shortage to a persisted warning episode. A responsive Vue interface gives administrators, managers and clerks access to different operations, while the Spring Boot server and the MySQL database remain responsible for authorization and durable change. Redis serves only as an optional page cache, never as a second source of business truth.

The first question asked how quantity changes can remain bounded, explainable and resistant to duplicates. The design answers it with a locked product read, server-derived arithmetic, a mandatory actor and reason, actor-scoped key uniqueness and a single coordinating transaction. Integration cases cover receipts, dispatches, corrections, absolute counts, rejected operations, replay and concurrency; in the concurrent-dispatch case, twelve attempts against seven units produce exactly seven successes and a final balance of zero.

The second question concerned the interpretation of warnings. The system keeps shortage, batch-age, slow-moving and recovery conditions apart from reviewer attribution. Tests cover zero stock and threshold equality, healthy replenishment, renewed shortage, batch expiry boundaries, sales-only slow-moving detection and concurrent acknowledgement, which records the first reviewer without altering stock. Clock-controlled tests of recovery expiry and cache visibility remain the most important gap in this part of the evaluation.

The third question concerned role-specific access. Endpoint rules separate catalog administration, routine stock posting and managerial review, browser navigation mirrors these boundaries, and integration cases confirm that unauthorized server requests are refused. The enabled flag and role are reloaded on every request. A wider deployment would add rate limiting, credential recovery, multi-factor authentication, shared session handling and a broader security assessment.

The fourth question concerned the evidence for performance and recovery. In the preserved warning-query benchmark of six hundred sequential samples per path, the pooled median is 5.33 ms with Redis enabled and 6.56 ms with the cache bypassed. The distributions overlap, and both paths include the revision and authentication work that the cache cannot remove. A recorded Redis interruption returned equivalent warning data, and an ordinary application restart preserved the selected stock and movement rows. These observations support the chosen local mechanisms but establish neither capacity, disaster recovery nor a production availability target.

The engineering contribution is the integration of audited stock changes, batch allocation, warning lifecycles and reviewed purchasing in a runnable single-store application, with requirements, source excerpts and test assertions exposing the relevant transaction and permission boundaries. The resulting records keep catalog edits, stock movements, physical observations and managerial decisions distinct.

Further development should address fractional quantities and rounding, event identity and reconciliation for point-of-sale integration, supplier terms and lead times, and multi-store isolation, each with its own ledger records and acceptance cases. Operational evaluation should examine real staff workflows, larger concurrent workloads, cache-expiry boundaries, cross-product key races, database deadlocks and restore procedures.

text: Every unsafe browser method requires a CSRF token in addition to the role checks listed. For purchase actions, the security filter only requires a signed-in user; the controller then applies the role check, because the permitted role depends on the action. Similarly, direct ADJUSTMENT and STOCKTAKE movements pass the filter for clerks but are refused by the transaction controller unless the caller is an administrator.

Paginated responses contain items, page, size, totalElements and totalPages. Product queries accept q, categoryId, status, archived, page, size, sort and direction, where status is one of healthy, low or out. Warning queries accept type, state, page, size and cache, and the controller rejects unsupported values. Timestamps are emitted in UTC as ISO-8601 strings and formatted in local time by the browser. {tab:status-codes} summarizes how clients should interpret each response status.

A transaction payload contains productId, type, quantity, reason and idempotencyKey, plus, where applicable, a batch number, production and expiry dates or a selected batch. Quantities for STOCK_IN, STOCK_OUT and SALE are positive, with STOCK_OUT and SALE reducing stock; ADJUSTMENT is signed and non-zero; STOCKTAKE is an absolute, non-negative count. A request to receive twelve units therefore carries no actor ID, quantityBefore or quantityAfter: the server derives these from the authenticated session and the locked product.
